$comment: The issue catalog: one index over every open item in this repo, and the
only place that knows they are the same kind of thing.
WHY THIS EXISTS. Open work was tracked in four registers that had never been
counted together: PLAN.md's numbered follow-ups (the roadmap of record),
backlog.md (unscheduled optimization), each design doc's open-questions
section, and validation/ledger.json (the checks a machine cannot run). Each
register was internally disciplined and none could see the others. The cost
was not theoretical: page-turning.md OE9 was found only because somebody
opened that document and read to the end, and nothing anywhere would have
noticed if it had been fixed in code and left marked `confirmed` in prose.
WHAT IT IS NOT. This file does not restate an issue. It carries no title, no
description, no reproduction — those live in the document that owns the item,
and a copy here would drift while still looking authoritative. That is the
same rule validation/ledger.json runs on and the same reason map.json points
at symbols instead of quoting them. What this file adds is the metadata no
single document can hold: severity, who owns it, what it blocks, what closed
it, and the fact that two registers are describing one item.
HOW A SOURCE IS READ. Every design doc under docs/design/ ends with a section
headed exactly `Open questions, and what would answer each`, and backlog.md's
body is one such register. Under both, an item is a heading of the form
### OEn <title> · **status**
so scripts/gate-issues.mjs finds items without knowing anything about the
document. `status` in this file must equal the marker in that heading; the
duplication IS the gate, in the same shape as the SOURCES.md <-> Colophon.tsx
licence-copy check.
TWO SOURCES ARE READ DIFFERENTLY, ON PURPOSE.
validation/ledger.json is already machine-readable and already gated. Its
checks are indexed here by id and their status is read from the ledger, not
copied — gate-validation.mjs stays the authority on them.
PLAN.md's follow-ups are NOT marked. They are compound narratives whose job
is to record how a thing was believed over time — follow-up 2 keeps its own
retracted licence claim beside the correction, and 10 carries three
successive re-measurements. Flattening one of those to a single word would
destroy the thing it is for. So a PLAN follow-up is indexed by number, the
gate checks only that the number still exists, and this file's `status` is
the summary rather than a checksum. That is the one special case and it is
written down rather than discovered.
STATUS VOCABULARY. Six words, defined once, here.
open       nobody has decided; no blocker named
confirmed  a defect, reproduced, with the numbers in its source
suspected  read from the code, never reproduced or profiled
blocked    the next step is named and unavailable (hardware, a hafiz, a loop)
answered   decided; nothing owed in code
fixed      closed in code AND in a test that would fail if it came back.
`closedBy` is required and the gate refuses the word without it —
the same standing rule the ledger runs on, that a result must
tighten something automated or it has not been banked.
SEVERITY. Three words. `defect` — the app does something wrong today.
`question` — a decision not yet made. `risk` — something unmeasured that
could be wrong, which is the category `suspected` items live in.
FIELDS
id         kebab slug, stable, referenced by blockedBy
source     {file, item} — a design/backlog OEn row, a PLAN follow-up number,
or {ledger: <check id>}
status     see above; must match the source marker except for ledger/PLAN
severity   defect | question | risk
owner      agent (doable from this machine) | user (needs a human or hardware)
blockedBy  ids in this file, ledger check ids, or a loop name
closedBy   required when status is `fixed`: the test or gate that notices a
regression. A path, and the gate checks it resolves.
make issues        the open items, grouped, worst first
make issues-doc    regenerate docs/issues.md (a gate checks it is not stale)
pnpm gate:issues   the invariants
the `issues` skill drives triage: pick, open, close

issues.note: Closed as three pieces: a plain wheel turns pages (§3.2 ④), ctrl+wheel is calibrated to a multiplicative curve, and desktop.md §6 finally documents the wheel. The headline claim was overstated — ctrl+wheel always fired — and the register keeps the wrong sentence beside the correction. STILL FIXED, HALF SUPERSEDED: the ctrl+wheel curve shipped, worked, and was then removed on the reader's call ('i don't want zoom to be driven by scrolling'). The calibration argument is left standing because it was correct about what it measured; the binding is gone, ctrl+wheel is now swallowed, and nextWheelTurn is reused verbatim for a Shift+wheel juz jump. The plain-wheel half — the actual headline of this item — is untouched. decisions/wheel-and-zoom.md.

No new string was needed for the skip, as the item predicted. The ends did need one: firstPage/lastPage now carry the page number, because 'last available page' alone leaves a reader guessing which of 604 they stopped at.

The proposal was reviewed and taken whole, Escape included — PageDown/PageUp give a way to turn, Escape gives a way back to the arrows. The ladder did not move: rule 3 still beats both, which is what keymap.test.ts is really asserting.

Deleted, not wired: page-transition.md §3.1 withdrew the cross-fade in favour of the fold, whose rule is that no glyph moves during a turn. 'answered' rather than 'fixed' on purpose — a test asserting the absence of a CSS rule proves nothing, so there is no test to name.

The one item in that document never reproduced — it carried `suspected` for six loops rather than borrowing a confidence it had not earned, and it was closed by a test rather than by the profile it asked for. Its own measurement was still never taken; what changed is that the heading's claim is now false. That measurement did not stop being worth taking, and it now tunes MOUNTED_PAGE_CAP rather than deciding whether a cap exists — which is backlog ① ②, blocked on hardware. Owned by backlog ③; indexed twice here on purpose, because two registers describing one item is exactly what this catalog exists to make visible.

Curiosity, not a blocker — SS4.6 fixes it constant here regardless. But if the reference does vary it, that is a design it got wrong for a memoriser.

±1. The arrow turns a page, at every width. The behaviour is unchanged and every reason for it is new: §6 argued from scarcity (±2 over an inventory of three is a no-op) and loop-4b deleted that argument. What holds now — stepPage must name any landing that is not the page next door, so ±2 would announce a correction on every turn (page-turning.md §7 ④); ±2 reaches one parity only, putting half the print out of reach of the arrows, for the reader with the fewest ways back to them; a keyed turn, a wheel turn and a dragged fold all end in one stepPage and would stop meaning the same thing; and appKeyAction would have to learn the window's width, which KeyContext deliberately cannot see. What made ±2 attractive — half the presses on a spread move no paper — is not a defect: both leaves of the opening are already open, and PageStage:855 already suppresses the fold for it. Reasoning is in keymap.ts; the pin is desktop.spec.ts's 'still turns pages with the arrow keys the header advertises', which reads 8 after one press and would read 9 under ±2.

Neither: above default zoom the book closes to the one leaf being read. The question offered two ways for two leaves to behave under a zoom and the reader reframed it — a spread is an offer of more of the book at once, and zooming is declining that offer in favour of one page. Panning was already answered and nobody had noticed: holdAxis centres any axis that fits, so at z<=1 a pan is a measured no-op. Three defects the running app had, found by screenshotting it rather than reading it: a cold ayah link left the two leaves at different scales (1.55 vs 1.0) with the selection band cut by the gutter; ctrl+wheel over the facing leaf zoomed the facing leaf, so hover was silently choosing the subject of the gesture against decision row 15; and a third — that zoom pushed the fore-edge outside the clip — was claimed from the screenshots and is FALSE, measured: ::after is inside the transformed host and travels with it, so at 2.07x the whole host sits inside the book's box. It thickens with the page, which the border does too and PageStage.module.css argues for. No issue filed; the wrong claim is kept beside the measurement in desktop.md. The shared View was rendered rather than argued about and reads as one continuous column, which an opening is not. The size argument for closing was WRONG and is kept beside its correction: .leaf is height-bound at ~398px whether one leaf or two are on the desk, so this buys no reading size — it buys the viewport, a page at 1.55x seen whole instead of through a 398px slot. Built as onFitChange on PageStage (flip, not frame; z <= 1+1e-3 because a tween's last frames arrive at 1.0000003) plus solo on PageSpread as style and not mount, and a ResizeObserver on the stage layer because the leaf now widens because of a zoom. Decision row 23. STILL FIXED, MECHANISM SUPERSEDED: the answer above survived and the way it was built did not. Deriving soloLeaf from zoom leaked three ways — ctrl+wheel over the facing leaf took it to 1.549 alone while the live leaf sat at 0.8 (the comment saying the facing leaf 'never receives a gesture that could change its own scale' was simply untrue, and is why nobody looked); a breakpoint crossing remounted the live stage and reset its view but not the mode, leaving data-solo=true over scale(1); and atFit's z <= 1+1e-3 against MIN_ZOOM 0.8 reopened the book at 266px beside 332px. One state with two owners has patches, not a fix. Page mode is now an explicit radiogroup and zoom an explicit stepper, disabled while the book is open — the same finding kept as an ordering of two controls instead of a derivation. onFitChange and atFitRef are deleted; the ResizeObserver stays, for the independent reason recorded here. Decision rows 25-27, decisions/wheel-and-zoom.md.

No. Landscape iPads (1194x834, 1080x810) clear the breakpoint on both axes and have no keyboard, so the item's trigger — wait for a bug report — was never going to fire. Still a proxy: no media feature reports a keyboard.

loop-4b dropped off the blocker list by happening: the second mount is real on every spread now, which is what made the risk measurable rather than hypothetical. It still cannot be answered without the on-device verdict, so the chain is one link shorter and not shorter than that.

Asked as a design question and answered as a defect: RevisionMap was the only one of eight sheets with no `@media (min-width: 900px)` rule, and at 1440px its auto-fill grid laid 30 juz out as a single row. Fixed with a bounded centred card plus a named column count per scope; the owed row in docs/decisions/desktop-vs-mobile.md is row 22.
A ledger candidate. The bands decide what `cold` means, and a threshold chosen by whoever wrote the renderer is a claim about somebody else's revision habit.

Answered by building it. A held cell is a button that opens its division on the lowest page of it this build holds — read off the manifest through the same scopesOf sweep that decides whether the cell is drawn, never off HIZB_STARTS, which knows the ayah and not the page of this print. coverage became holdings and returns a map instead of a set. The announcer says «الحزب ٣ · صفحة ٢٢» at hizb and juz scope and nothing extra at page scope, where the cell and the landing are one fact. An absent cell stays a plain li with no control at all. The grid is one tab stop, not 604, via a roving tabindex — and page-scope cells meet WCAG 2.5.8 by the equivalent-control exception (the jumper), not by size.

Latent rather than hypothetical: one edition is vendored, but an IndexedDB record outlives the build, so stored page ids would join the next print's grid silently. comparableEvents partitions at page scope only — a juz is the same in every print, and filtering there would show a hafiz less revision than they did.
37 forms Arabic silently substitutes today. One JSON edit each, but the edit needs a hafiz's eye. Named in its source as a known defect, deliberately deferred.

`I18n.other` deleted; both switches now render LOCALE_IDS from LOCALES. Behaviour-preserving at two locales — the registry's order is the order the hand-written buttons were in — so it was done without a third locale to render blind at. LOCALES gained `abbr` for the header. Tests in i18n.test.tsx and DesktopChrome.test.tsx are written over LOCALE_IDS, so they fail the day ur.json lands.

A real limit of interpolation, not a defect: the repair for a locale that inflects the inserted name is a different message, authorable only by someone who speaks the offering language. The same onset windows, re-read after it, gave tatweel-carrier (172 → 143, and a last 12 → 11 for the rare noon carrier), small-madda (60 → 19) and hamza-below (19 → 12). The narrowness is measured rather than chosen — generalising the tatweel rule to every U+0640 scores 94.48%, WORSE than applying nothing. Opened 2026-08-07 by probe-encodings.mjs on its first full pass, and it is the first thing the inspector found that nothing else could. The fold's residual is not scattered: offsets are cumulative, so one divergent codepoint pushes every later annotation in its ayah by the same amount, and 166 of the 172 residual ayahs carry exactly ONE delta throughout. That property makes the window between the last oracle hit and the first miss a localiser, and the words standing in those windows are one orthographic family — ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ in 41 of the 41 ayahs it appears in, ٱلۡأٓخِرِ 16/16, ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَ 9/9, ٱلۡأٓيَٰتُ 3/3, ٱلۡأٓخِرَ 3/3, لَأٓتِيَةٞ 2/2, every window bounded on both sides, every delta −1. All of them contain U+0623 ALEF WITH HAMZA ABOVE + U+0653 MADDAH ABOVE: the print spells أٓ in two codepoints where the text the tajweed offsets index spells it in three. That is 275 of the 475 misses, 57.89%, in one shape. What this does NOT have is the other side of the comparison — Tanzil's spelling is in a text this repo does not hold, so 'three codepoints' is inferred from arithmetic and not read. Two smaller families are visible in the same table and are the same kind of claim: U+0640 TATWEEL + U+06E7 SMALL HIGH YEH at +1 (ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ 3/3, يُحۡـِۧيَ 2/2, إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ 6 ayahs), and U+06E4 SMALL HIGH MADDA (يَسۡجُدُۤ 3/3, ٱسۡجُدُواْۤ 3/3). Worth recording separately: the +1 bucket had been attributed to the tatweel before this tool existed, on the strength of U+0640 occurring 535 times in the corpus, and the onset table says the bucket is heterogeneous and the tatweel is a minority of it — a plausible untested attribution corrected by the first run. What would answer it is a fourth entry in CORRECTIONS and a re-run; the oracle is the referee, because a wrong expansion makes it WORSE rather than silently better. Left to whoever owns the tajweed bake — the inspector's job is to show what is true, not to be right.

ANSWERED 2026-08-07, and the answer is no — it was correction 5 arriving, not the source. Measured on both folds rather than reasoned about: on the three structural corrections there are 90 lam_shamsiyyah misses of which 21 begin on ٱ, across 19 ayahs, reproducing this row exactly; on all seven there are 7 misses of which ONE begins on ٱ, at 36:52, which probe-tajweed-words.mjs's NAMED list already carries on other grounds. So the observation was sound and the attribution was not: those 19 ayahs are ٱلۡأٓخِرَة / إِبۡرَٰهِـۧم territory throughout, and what looked like a span starting one letter early was the أٓ drift already accumulated by the time the fold reached them. Nothing is owed upstream and nothing is owed in the bake. The lesson outlasts the row and is why it is kept rather than deleted: a drift of exactly one letter reads as an off-by-one in whoever wrote the span, because that is the most available explanation and it points away from your own code. The only thing separating it from the true reading is re-measuring under a different correction set — which is exactly what alef-maddah-is-a-fourth-correction's toggle mechanism bought, and the reason the corrections are a parameter rather than an edit. Before filing any future finding as upstream, switch corrections off and watch whether it grows. ORIGINAL NOTE FOLLOWS. 21 lam_shamsiyyah annotations across 19 ayahs (2:124, 2:126, 2:127, 2:130, 2:132, 2:136, 2:213, 2:260, …) miss the oracle at +1 with the drift shape exactly ٱ — the source's span begins on the alef wasla rather than on the ل the rule is named for. Suspected upstream in tajweed.hafs.uthmani-pause-sajdah.json rather than in the fold, because the same rule lands correctly on the alignment everywhere else and because these are all ٱل + a sun letter. Not confirmed: it would take reading the source's raw entries for those 19 against controls where the rule lands right, which the inspector's drill-down makes one click of work. If it is a source defect the fix is a named exception list in the bake, in the shape segmentation.mjs already uses for its four orthographic exceptions — NOT a widened oracle, which would buy coverage by making the check unable to see the next one.

FIXED 2026-08-07. All eighteen rules are in ORACLE; coverage is 60057/60057 = 100.00% of annotations and the hit rate is 59975/60057 = 99.863%, 82 misses across 10 ayahs, every one named. The widening was done the way this row said to do it — each letter set written from the tajweed rule FIRST and measured second, never read off where the offsets happened to land — and each entry carries the reason it has its shape in a required `why` field a test asserts is non-empty. The row's own warning was borne out twice. `iqlab` written as the high meem U+06E2 alone scored 85.05%, a reject by this repo's criterion; the 84 unreachable misses all had the shape «ِۭ ب», because the mark is written LOW (U+06ED) under a kasra and HIGH over a fatha or damma. With both it is 562/562 — the oracle catching its own letter set, which is precisely the failure this row named. And the headline number needed a companion: a hit rate alone is not evidence, because breadth is free — {ا,و,ي} is ~12% of the corpus, so a rule restricted to it would score well on a fold that was simply wrong. `oracleDensity(cps, rule)` measures what fraction of positions in an ayah would have satisfied the rule; 1 − density is the chance the check notices a one-codepoint drift, and both probes now weight by it. Sensitivity-weighted the coverage is 93.65%, not 100%, and `madd_6` (fifteen letters, 30% of the ayahs it appears in, 69.6% sensitivity, 148 annotations) says in its own `why` that it is the entry to distrust. Two sets were then corrected BY the residual rather than the reverse: ikhfa gained U+06E8 SMALL HIGH NOON (نۨجي writes the hidden noon small) and silent gained ص (the sin/sad alternate, where the letter written is not the letter read, which is what silent means). Both are marked data-led in their own `why`, because they were added after the residual pointed at them rather than written blind like the other sixteen, and the fix for a fit is to say so rather than hide it. The widening also paid the dividend this row doubted it would: correction 8, `sakta-seen`, is a substitution that was measured and REJECTED under the two-rule oracle (worth 1 annotation, 0 ayahs — 36:52 in probe-tajweed-words' NAMED) and is worth three ayahs under the eighteen-rule one, because silent, qalqalah, madd_246 and idghaam_shafawi had no vote when it was first weighed. ORIGINAL NOTE FOLLOWS. The oracle checks two of the source's eighteen rules — hamzat_wasl must start on ٱ, lam_shamsiyyah on ل — because those are the only two naming a letter whose identity is not in doubt. That is 15,985 of 60,057 annotations, 26.6%, and the headline 99.81% is 99.81% OF THAT QUARTER; the other 73.4% inherit a verdict they cannot witness. Several remaining rules have nearly characteristic letters (qalqalah on ق ط ب ج د, idghaam_ghunnah on ي ن م و) and admitting them would raise coverage a lot. Opened by loop-4b's 92 MB commit, and answered in it. 98.6% of a page is path d data, one <path> holds the whole scripture, and there is no font, use or symbol anywhere — the file is a photograph of the print, not a document. Shipped by loop-4b and not noticed in it: the page bar drew its inventory as one span per vendored page, which was three marks at three pages and 604 half-pixel-apart marks at 604 — a solid rail conveying nothing, reconciled on every value a dragged thumb passed over, on the component whose commit-on-release design exists to avoid paying per value. Proven twice: the core helper in pages.test.ts and the rendered DOM in apps/web/src/components/PageSlider.test.tsx.

Found by the 6b-D pack e2e and by nothing else: the assertion that page 15 lives in the pack and nowhere else came back naming hifth-pages too. pinPack fetched from the page, so the service worker's CacheFirst route stored every file a second time — juz 1's ~3.1 MB paid twice, and 21 of the 32 entries in a browsing-sized LRU spent on duplicates, so keeping a juz for later threw away most of what the reader read last week. Fixed 2026-08-04: pinPack sends X-Hifth-Pin and both runtimeCaching routes decline anything carrying it. Both reasons for deferring it turned out to be wrong under measurement — sweeping on unpin cannot work at all, because ExpirationPlugin evicts at write time (31 trail entries, 11 survive a 21-page pin, still 11 after deleting all 21 duplicates), and the 'pack knowledge in the worker' cost was mispriced: the worker gains one bit of static provenance and never learns the pack cache's name, its URL list, or that a register exists. Proven by a new e2e that compares the hifth-pages key set across a pin, plus the ⑮ tripwire flipped from [PACK_CACHE, hifth-pages] to [PACK_CACHE]; negative control run and reverted. Not verified outside Chromium — if a browser hides the header from FetchEvent.request the failure mode is the old duplicate, not a broken pack, and that check sits on the offline-survival device runbook.

Reproduced 2026-08-06 with two curl lines against the deployed site: http:// returns 200 and the whole app in cleartext — not a redirect — and the https response carries no Strict-Transport-Security. The security half is ordinary; the half that made it a backlog row is that a service worker needs a secure context, so an http arrival hits pwa.ts:270's `if (!("serviceWorker" in navigator)) return` and gets a mushaf that paints and hops correctly with no precache, no pinned juz and no offline, and nothing on screen to tell it apart from the build that has them — Loop 6b's whole promise, absent and unfalsifiable from the inside. Every offline check we own runs against localhost, which browsers treat as secure regardless of scheme, so the suite is green on a configuration that fails in the field: the same blind spot /validate's probes section is about. The fix is two toggles in the Cloudflare zone (Always Use HTTPS, then HSTS) and there is no token on this machine, nor should there be. Verified by curl returning 301 with an https location, and strict-transport-security on the https response; it will never be a gate, because it reaches the network and the deployed origin is not reproducible from a commit.

The only check that can establish the scripture data is correct. Narrowed on 2026-08-06 without being closed: scripts/probe-reference.mjs settles the arithmetic underneath it from a third party — all 604 pages of our ayah→page table against api.quran.com's, 568 agree and 36 diverge exactly where V1/1405H and V2/1421H are known to, 0 surprises — so 'is this ayah on the page we print beside it?' is no longer part of what a human is being asked. What is left is the whole of the judgement: whether an edge joins two ayahs a hafiz would actually confuse. No reachable source answers that, which is why this stays owner:user and severity:risk rather than moving. The probe is deliberately not a gate (it reaches the network) and its measurement is banked in packages/etl/data/pages/PROVENANCE.md; .claude/skills/mushaf-reference/SKILL.md names which published references can stand in for paper and which will make a correct pair look wrong.

The runnable half of nobody-has-looked-at-the-placement-verdicts: that row is the question, this row is the twenty minutes that answers it. Built 2026-08-08 — `pnpm adjudicate:marks` renders a hundred blind two-panel trials over forty pages, and `pnpm adjudicate:score` rebuilds the key from the seed afterwards, so nothing on disk knew the answers while they were being given. Deliberately a forced choice rather than a list of verdicts with agree/disagree beside each: a person shown a machine's verdict agrees with it, and what comes back is the machine's own opinion wearing a human's name. It is a risk rather than a question because mark-C cannot ship on an uninspected correction. Wired into `make session CHECK=placement-correction-by-eye` on 2026-08-12: opened from a session the trials post each answer straight into that sitting's transcript and bank the ruling file at the end, so the twenty minutes cannot end in a download nobody can find. Still says nothing about how it is going, because it still does not know.

The other half hour, and it asks a question the first one cannot. A forced choice returns a preference — our rectangle beat the one it was shown against — and a correction that points the right way and falls a third short wins every trial while still being wrong. Built 2026-08-12: `pnpm nudge:marks` renders one rectangle per trial, starting a fixed distance out in a direction that changes every time, and the reader puts it where it belongs; `pnpm nudge:score` subtracts what the machine proposed from where it was actually put, and what is left is a magnitude in units. It reports that against the reader's OWN precision, measured in the same sitting from marks shown twice, because a residual smaller than the hand that produced it is not a finding. Deliberately a second session rather than a drag handle on the first: adjusting a rectangle inside a two-panel trial and then scoring the landing against the two starting positions IS the answer key, and adjusting after answering teaches the direction of the correction, which points the same way on nearly every page. The two should not be worked back to back by the same person. Risk rather than question because mark-C's thresholds are a claim about magnitude and only this can check one.

The third sitting, and the first one that can be wrong. Its two predecessors both drew every trial from the same forty pages the correction was worked out on, because a trial needs a proposed move to start from and only those forty had one — so between them they could establish that the correction points the right way and nothing else. Built 2026-08-12 once all 604 pages carried a measurement: the builder now takes the pages to draw from as an argument, will hold out the pages an earlier sitting used, and picks by preference from the pages wanting the largest and smallest moves rather than at random. That last part is the whole point — across the original forty the proposed moves spanned 0.31 units of which most was noise, and across the held-out forty it spans 1.75 across and 3.38 down, four to six times the leverage per placement, which is the difference between being able to read the SIZE of the correction and not. Two blocks, deliberately on pages that do not overlap: forty-seven placements over forty held-out pages for whether it travels, and twenty-three over five pages at four or five each for how much of the leftover belongs to the page rather than to the hand — the second thing being what the clustered interval currently has to assume the worst about. Neither block has the correction applied to it: applying it first would make a genuine nought indistinguishable from a coincidence and would bake an unresolved number into the instrument measuring it. FOUR PREDICTIONS ARE BANKED IN THE LEDGER BEFORE ANYBODY PLACES ANYTHING, which is the part that makes this a check rather than an exercise — direction at 90% or better, the leftover returning either near (-0.073, -0.110) or near nought, the size estimate at 1.0 with an interval a fifth of a unit wide, and the between-page spread exceeding the within-page one. Each says in the ledger what its own failure would mean. What this still cannot answer is whether the leftover is a fact about the print or about one reader; only a second person placing the same rectangles separates those, and that block is designed in the plan and not built. Scoring is guarded twice over: the answers carry a fingerprint of the displacements AND of the chosen pages, and the scorer refuses a displacements file that has no row for a page the sitting used, because a file can carry the right fingerprint and still be the wrong file for these pages. Risk rather than question for the same reason as its neighbours: mark-C cannot ship on a correction judged only where it was fitted.

The fourth sitting, and the first one that does not answer in a distance. Its three predecessors all ask how far — is our rectangle preferred to the one beside it, how far does a reader move it, does either answer survive on a page the correction never measured — and a distance is the right currency right up to the point where the best correction places most rectangles from their own ink and the remainder stops being rectangles that are merely far out. Measured over the whole book: where a rectangle was placed from its own ink the printed strokes fill about a fifth of it and roughly one in eighty is effectively bare; where the match was weak it is a ninth and more than a QUARTER are bare; where the best match sat on the edge of how far the search was allowed to look it is a twentieth and more than a THIRD are bare. About a third of what is left is a rectangle over blank paper, and no distance can say `there is nothing in this place`. Nor can one separate right-place-wrong-size from right-size-wrong-place — two faults with two repairs in two files, and a size complaint written as a displacement is a wrong number that looks like a right one. Built 2026-08-13: `pnpm report:marks` draws sixty of them one at a time, each croppable between the whole word and a close look because the first attempt at this was stopped after one screen for not being able to tell WHICH letter a mark belonged to, and the reader answers in words from a vocabulary of five — move it, wrong shape, box the right ink instead, the print is odd, bank it. As many as are true, not one: forced to pick one a reader picks the most obvious and the second fault is never recorded by anybody, which is the deliberate break from all three earlier sittings. Two of the five carry their own rules. Wrong shape carries no coordinates and never will, for the reason above. The print is odd is the only answer on the page that is not about us — we did not draw those pages — and it routes into THIS catalog as rows of its own rather than into any ruling that grades a correction, because counted as a placement failure a printing oddity makes our correction look worse than it is and counted the other way, better. The page reports how many are left and nothing else: no score, no running share, no verdict, because a reader who can see the score answers the score. Risk rather than question because both readings of the tail in mark-registration.md §⑩ ⑨ are live — if most of the remainder is the print then every error figure in that document overstates our own by that share, and if most of it is rectangles that could have been placed and were not then the search is too timid and that is a change to make. Widened the same day into TWO sittings of sixty, and the second one is the one that matters most: everything above is about the six in a thousand the correction refuses to place, and the other 99.4% — every rectangle put where its own printed ink is — has never been looked at by anybody. Its only evidence is a held-out split, which defends against a correction that fits noise and not at all against one that is confidently wrong the same way everywhere, since the ink is both what it was fitted to and the only thing that has ever been asked. Three faults in sixty there is a few per cent of 324,638 marks, which is thousands, and a fact about the whole book; the identical share in the tail is a rounding error. The two are never pooled and there is no combined figure, here or in the scorer: the populations differ in size by a factor of 173, so a rate over both would be a fact about how many of each the sampler happened to draw. `pnpm report:score` reads each ruling, re-derives which population every answer came from rather than believing the file, prints an interval beside every share because sixty marks cannot tell one in fifty from one in seven, and takes the marks called odd in the print out of the denominator rather than into the numerator — printing the rate both ways so the size of that choice is visible.
Substantially closed. What is still live: the Libyan Endowments editions are non-commercial-only, so EditionPicker may not grow one of those rows on the strength of hafs-kfqc's terms.

Vendored 2026-08-04 — the boxes shipped and this item is spent. build-words.mjs transferred 91,451 word rectangles onto our frame as 604 shards (886 KB gz, ceiling 1792) with a SHA-256 per upstream page and per shard in word-boxes.pin.json; 378 MB was read and no upstream byte ships. Residual over all 604: median 0.089, max 2.722 (p1, the override frame), against measured ceilings of 2.0 standard / 3.0 override. The one prediction still standing that turned out to matter is not in this note at all: the word index is the print's, not the Quranic Arabic Corpus's, and the two disagree on 4,499 of 6,236 ayahs because the print counts pause marks as words — so word-granular roots and tajweed painting needs an alignment between the two segmentations, which is the remaining piece of task #65 and is tracked there. And the second print earned its keep twice: gate:words re-measures every box offline with its own parser and found a defect gate:pages structurally could not — on p577 the ink of 75:5's first word was covered by a tappable box, the wrong ayah's, so there was no orphan for an orphan check to find. One misplaced word in 86,965; repaired in vendor-pages.mjs as a fourth defect shape and now zero. Registration answer follows. Registration answered 2026-08-04, and it closes this item rather than moving the wall again — the prediction recorded below, that no word box transfers without a per-page registration against the text block, is wrong twice. packages/etl/scripts/probe-word-registration.mjs fits ours = s*theirs + t on a correspondence both corpora already carry and neither was built to provide: the ayah-end ornaments (ours <g ayah:x ayah:y>, theirs <g id=md-aya-mark-NNN data-surah data-aya>), 5-20 exact point pairs per page, no fonts and no rendering. #md-page-inner's data-rect is never read. Over 61 pages the scale is 1.3333 in both axes everywhere, ty is a constant near -88.6, and tx takes exactly two values — -114.6 on even pages, -54.6 on odd — the recto/verso binding margin, and the same two constants already sitting in our own SVGs' transform matrices. The registration was in the repo the whole time. Marker residual median 0.104 / max 0.506 viewBox units = 0.10-0.63 device pixels at 320-430 px, so the per-page fit is a check and not a necessity, and 'vendor the boxes, not the pictures' survives with the 67 MB never fetched. Two lessons banked because both produced confident wrong answers first: document order is not reading order (pairing on emitted order fits a mirror — negative x-scale, residual 157 on p575), and the ayah polygons sit outside the flipping matrix, which is why registering against them gives a positive scale rather than a flip. Task #65 is unblocked. What the probe found on the way is a defect in our own data and is indexed separately as plan-ayah-polygon-misses-its-ayah. Print answer follows. Answered 2026-08-04 — V2, the same print we ship. packages/etl/scripts/probe-ligature-print.mjs ran the arithmetic wider than the follow-up proposed: every page of all four known V1/V2 divergence bands (120-123, 144-145, 531-534, 564-600) plus controls either side of each band and at both ends of the book, 56 pages, 56/56 with an ayah span identical to ayah-pages.json. The controls are the half that makes it a finding rather than a coincidence — contested pages alone cannot separate 'this corpus is V2' from 'our own table is wrong in exactly the contested places'. So the YES branch holds and word granularity needs a second vendoring — but the probe replaced one blocker with another rather than clearing the way. Three things it found that the follow-up did not predict: weight (595 KB raw / 114 KB gz per page, 67 MB gz for 604, against the 26.2 MB the app ships today and gate:assets' 32 MB projection ceiling); shape (per-word groups wrap per-ligature <path data-text>, so a word's box is measured or precomputed, never read off an attribute); and coordinates (our p120 is viewBox 0 0 345 550 under matrix(1.3333 0 0 -1.3333 -115 640), theirs is viewBox 0 0 382.68 547.09 with data-rect on #md-page-inner — same print, different frame, so no word box transfers without a per-page registration against the text block). Which points at vendoring boxes rather than pictures: derive per-word rects in ETL, register them onto the shipped frame, ship a manifest beside ayah-pages.json. Does not unblock task #65 by itself; it retargets it from a corpus hunt to registration. Original note follows. Opened by loop-4b, which decided it NO on evidence rather than deferring it unexamined. Half is settled: the adopted corpus carries one polygon per ayah and nothing finer, so word granularity cannot come from the pages that now ship. The other half is a print question, not a licence or a size question — the candidate ligature corpus has per-ligature groups, 604 pages, KFGQPC Hafs and a permissive licence, and its README does not say which print. loop-4a's finding is what makes that decisive: V1/1405H and V2/1421H disagree on 36 pages, and adopting a V1-paginated corpus would silently invalidate ayah-pages.json, every edge's dPage and every share link. Adopting it is a second corpus, not a layer. What would answer it is named in the follow-up and is an afternoon: run 4a's arithmetic against the candidate and check whether 5:77 sits on its p120 and 5:83 on its p121. Blocks word-level selection (task #65) and the word-granular roots and tajweed painting that Loops 5 and 6a left at ayah fallback.

Repaired 2026-08-04, and eleven pages were seven short. Before writing a repair the detector was rebuilt on the principle that a repair validated by the signatures that found the defect proves only that the signatures were satisfied: the new one maps every glyph through the page matrix and asks whether its centre falls inside some polygon. It found seven more — 227, 294, 468, 542, 549, 558, 560 — and the reason the old rule missed four of them is one clause, `bands[0].ayah !== 1`, which excused any page whose first polygon is an X:1 on the correct observation that a surah header pushes the first polygon down. Correct about headers, wrong about p542 (58:1, one abandoned line), p549 (60:1, four) and p558 (65:1, three), which have a header AND an abandoned run above the ayah's only rect. The other three are a shape the old rule did not model: a rect off the line grid (28.8 or 46.2 where the print sets 36), so its top edge cuts through a line instead of sitting between two. Missing rects are placed from the page's own line pitch, taken as the MODAL rect height and not the median — a squashed rect is itself the defect and would lead the estimator — and 15 lines to a page, so blockTop = lastRectBottom - 15*pitch. Two traps recorded so they are not re-learnt: upstream gives a surah's X:1 polygon a ~12-unit sliver at the LEFT MARGIN on the line the previous surah ended, ABOVE the header (p106 5:1 at y152.25 while its header band is 188.25-260.25), so a furniture window anchored at 'where the ayah-1 polygon starts' measures 0.00 lines and invents 69-99 orphans on p106/255/440/467/515; and the tolerance is measured, not chosen — benign glyphs sit at most 8.8 units outside their box, real defects a median 36, so 12 separates them and the gate can demand ZERO rather than carry a count that would absorb the next defect. gate-pages.mjs now runs two tests, ORPHAN and BAND, both at zero, with NO allow-list at all: it knows nothing of the repair table, so a regressed repair and a newly-broken upstream fail identically. 18 pages before, 0 after. The repairs are POLYGON_REPAIRS in vendor-pages.mjs — 21 edits over 18 pages, because moving a rect on 294/468/560 moves the neighbouring ayah's too — declared as the third transform beside svgo and ID_REPAIRS, each carrying the exact upstream `d` it replaces so a fixed upstream dies loudly, and applied BEFORE svgo because svgo rewrites path data at floatPrecision 1. The re-vendor changed exactly those 18 files, the Loop 0 self-test still reproduces pages 7/9/19 byte-for-byte, and the pin moved only in its vendored hashes. Proof is the probe this started in: 245 ordinary words adrift before, 7 after, all on page 1 — the decorated Fatiha frame, the one page with an override transform and the 2.72 residual PLAN 14 records as still unexplained, and the page the coverage gate skips by name because every line-pitch statement is false of it. Detection and the original report follow. An ayah's tap target does not always cover the ayah — wrong in the app today at ayah granularity, which is why it is indexed apart from plan-word-geometry-is-a-second-corpus even though that probe found it. Eleven pages, by two signatures a gate can test: `leading` (545, 551, 554, 564, 566, 575, 594, 599) where an ayah flowing in from the previous page loses its first line or five — p545's 58:22 loses five, 50 words untappable, and p575's 73:20 loses six and 77; and `gap` (431, 602, 604) where a strip between two bands is uncovered and the band below is not an X:1. Detection landed 2026-08-04 in scripts/gate-pages.mjs as an allow-list of exactly those eleven, so a twelfth fails and so does a repaired one. PLAN 14 carries the full account, including the withdrawal of its own first report — a scan that decomposed polygons into axis-aligned rectangles wrongly condemned pages 1 and 2, which are fine; 118 polygons in this corpus are general polygons and 11 of them are on those two pages. That count itself read 189 until it was re-measured on 2026-08-04 and found wrong at the commit that wrote it — float equality, not drift: the corpus writes rectangles relative, 80.6 + 184 - 184 is 80.59999999999997, and 71 of the 189 were rectangles whose closing edge missed by 3e-14. gate:pages now counts and prints both the subpath total and the general-polygon total on every run rather than asserting them in a comment. Still owed: the repair, which is upstream in the polygon metadata vendor-pages.mjs reads (confirmed against 545.json at the pinned commit) and needs a declared repair pass, a re-vendor and a re-pin. Blocks nothing; breaks reading now.

Fixed 2026-08-05 by word-D, in the order the note below predicted and with one deliberate departure from it. The blocker went first: the alignment landed, a word run now refines the hop list, and only then did the keyboard path get built — Enter on an already-selected ayah descends, ←/→ carry the run, Shift extends it, Escape climbs one rung. The departure is the announcement. This note said it should name the run's first and last word; what shipped counts the outcome instead — «٧ مواضع مشابهة», how many places the run is about — because naming the words means putting scripture in a UI string, which is the one thing the word grain exists not to do (word-indexing.md §10, and §11 ② for the argument).
